source: Prochaska, Vera, Tan, Starbird (2024) Misleading Ourselves: How Disinformation Manipulates Sensemaking (CHI 2024 Sensemaking workshop paper)
finding: Defines manipulated sensemaking: disinformation works by disrupting how audiences derive meaning from novel or ambiguous data, not only by adding false facts. Disinformation shapes broad deep stories, and deep stories set the frames used on new events.
numbers: Qualitative coding of about 1000 tweets: 5 salient rumors per election, 100 tweets per rumor, about 500 per year (2020 and 2022). Keyword and date-range sampling that mixed highly spread tweets with general talk. No effect sizes, no inter-coder statistics, no human-subject experiment.
limits: Workshop paper, preliminary results, one domain (US election rumors), one platform (Twitter), one political direction. No control or counterfactual.
agent_relevance: The claim is that the attack is on the frame, not the fact. For an agent, input hygiene must cover what frame a source sets, not only whether each claim is true.
quote: Disinformation isn't an information-level attack, it's a "meaning" level attack

source: Prochaska, Vera, Tan, Starbird (2024) Misleading Ourselves: How Disinformation Manipulates Sensemaking (CHI 2024 Sensemaking workshop paper) - claim 1: plausibility over accuracy
finding: Authors say sensemaking is driven by plausibility, and the bar for plausibility is far lower than the bar for accuracy. Good for acting fast; a weakness when someone is feeding the process.
numbers: Section 4.3. Audiences shared stories to judge whether there was a threat, with a functional goal (audits, firing officials, rallies, #StopTheSteal) rather than abstract understanding.
limits: Interpretive claim from coded tweets. Not tested against an accuracy-oriented condition.
agent_relevance: An LLM that picks the most coherent story among cues has the same weakness. A coherence score is not an accuracy score.
quote: the bar of proof for plausibility is much lower than the bar established by accuracy

source: Prochaska, Vera, Tan, Starbird (2024) Misleading Ourselves: How Disinformation Manipulates Sensemaking (CHI 2024 Sensemaking workshop paper) - claim 2: deep stories constrain frame choice
finding: Deep stories (Hochschild's idea, adapted by Polletta and Callahan) are a set of related frames, not one frame. They narrow which frames people try on new data. This is a softer version of Klein's frame fixation.
numbers: Frames seen across rumors: election like a third-world election; censorship by media and tech firms; suspicion of government and voting technology. In Maricopa 2022 the frame switched from voter fraud to voter disenfranchisement, while villains and blame stayed the same.
limits: Window-frame and support-beam metaphor is illustrative, not a formal model. Number of frames was not measured.
agent_relevance: A deep story is a prior over frames. In the schema this is a hidden prior carried by the context, which S1 could strip or flag.

source: Prochaska, Vera, Tan, Starbird (2024) Misleading Ourselves: How Disinformation Manipulates Sensemaking (CHI 2024 Sensemaking workshop paper) - claim 3: deep stories persist and need only be cued
finding: A deep story built in 2020 was only referenced in 2022. Elites made explicit fraud claims much less often in 2022 and relied on audiences to interpret events through the old story. Authors say this cut the number of frames audiences used.
numbers: Appendix 1 lists 10 coded incidents: 5 from 2020 (USPS 300,000 undelivered ballots, Ilhan Omar ballot harvesting, Michigan dead voters, Hammer and Scorecard, Dominion) and 5 from 2022 (Konnech, Lake amplifies personal stories, Maricopa broken machines, treasurer vs governor votes, USPS DeJoy). No count of the frame reduction is reported.
limits: Reduction in frames is asserted, not quantified. A later paper, Deep storytelling (Prochaska 2025), reportedly finds 2020 spelled out fraud mechanics and 2022 relied on allusion; seen only in a secondary index entry, not opened.
agent_relevance: Priming by earlier turns: a stale frame in a long context may act as a cue without being stated. Test with equal-token masked vs unmasked contexts.

source: Prochaska, Vera, Tan, Starbird (2024) Misleading Ourselves: How Disinformation Manipulates Sensemaking (CHI 2024 Sensemaking workshop paper) - worked cases: Sharpie and Box 3
finding: Real, ordinary events were read as fraud. In 2020 Maricopa, Sharpie bleed-through was read as an intentional act against conservative voters, although ballots were designed for Sharpies and votes were not invalidated. In 2022 tabulator errors and the Box 3 procedure were read as fraud though the remedy was normal.
numbers: No counts of readers who accepted the reading. Credibility signals named: repetition by in-group members (Foster 2022) and source authority (Lin et al. 2016).
limits: Same kind of data, one frame. Only coded tweets, not a measured belief shift.
agent_relevance: Shows ambiguous cues being routed through a prior story. A test for an agent: feed identical ambiguous facts under two different prior narratives and compare the reading.

source: Prochaska, Duskin, Kharazian, Minow, Blucker, Venuto, West, Starbird (2023) Mobilizing Manufactured Reality: How Participatory Disinformation Shaped Deep Stories to Catalyze Action during the 2020 U.S. Presidential Election (PACM HCI 7 CSCW1)
finding: Three 2020 cases (Sonoma County ballot dumping, Sharpiegate in Maricopa, Dominion in Antrim County) show influencers and ordinary users jointly building evidence that fit a voter-fraud deep story. Offline acts (protests, affidavits) then became new evidence, a self-reinforcing loop.
numbers: Three cases. The summary page gave no dataset counts. The full PDF could not be fetched (NSF PAR refused the connection, ACM returned 403).
limits: Opened only the university summary page, not the full paper, so counts and coding detail are missing. Interpretive, mixed-method.
agent_relevance: Loop to guard against: model output or an action taken becomes cited evidence for the next turn. Fits G2 (revise only from real output).

source: Weick (1995) Sensemaking in Organizations; Weick (1993) The collapse of sensemaking in organizations: the Mann Gulch disaster
finding: Seven properties of sensemaking, including identity, social, and driven by plausibility rather than accuracy. Mann Gulch (1949): sensemaking collapsed when expected order failed. Prochaska 2024 uses this as its base.
numbers: Not read this session; described via Prochaska 2024 section 2.1.
limits: Not opened. Case-study theory, no experiments.
agent_relevance: Plausibility-driven stopping is the default failure; the schema needs a check that is not plausibility.

source: Klein, Phillips, Rall, Peluso (2007) A data-frame theory of sensemaking
finding: Data-frame theory: elements are explained by fitting them into a frame, and the frame decides which data count. Frame fixation is the error of being stuck on one explanation. Prochaska 2024 extends it by adding the deep story as a structure behind frames.
numbers: Not read. Covered in depth in subfield 01_data_frame_theory_and_frame_activities; not repeated here.
limits: Not opened. The deep-story extension is a proposal, not a test of the model.
agent_relevance: See subfields 01 and 03 for fixation. The only new point here is that the frame can be planted by a third party.

source: Hochschild (2016) Strangers in Their Own Land; Polletta and Callahan (2019) Deep stories, nostalgia narratives, and fake news: storytelling in the Trump era
finding: Deep story: a feels-as-if story that traded in feelings more than confirmable facts. Polletta and Callahan add three traits: allusiveness (the moral is not stated), social storytelling, collective identity building.
numbers: Not read; described via Prochaska 2024 section 2.3.
limits: Not opened. Ethnographic and sociological, not experimental.
agent_relevance: Allusiveness means a manipulating text may never state its frame. A keyword filter will miss it.

source: Kapferer (1990/2013) Rumors: Uses, Interpretations, and Images
finding: A rumor is defined by its unofficial source, not by being false. Rumors often take the form of exemplary stories that illustrate a larger suspected truth. Rumors fit a moment and can fade.
numbers: Not read; described via Prochaska 2024 section 2.2.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Source status (unconfirmed, no official denial) is a usable input flag, independent of truth value.

source: Johnson and Seifert (1994) Sources of the continued influence effect: when misinformation in memory affects later inferences
finding: Classic human result behind plausibility over accuracy: a retracted causal explanation still shapes later inferences unless a replacement explanation fills the causal gap. Stated from memory of the literature, not opened.
numbers: Exact figures not read.
limits: Not opened; numbers withheld. Replications and boundary conditions (Ecker et al. 2022, Lewandowsky 2012) belong to the other-angle files.
agent_relevance: If the agent drops a bad premise it needs a replacement cause, not a bare deletion. Link to the Anomalies and Belief updating subfields.

source: Xie, Zhang, Chen, Lou, Su (2024) Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: Revealing the Behavior of LLMs in Knowledge Conflicts (ICLR 2024)
finding: With coherent, LLM-written counter-evidence as the only source, models mostly accept it over their own memory. Crude entity-swap evidence is mostly rejected. So coherence, not truth, drives acceptance.
numbers: Models: ChatGPT, GPT-4, PaLM2, Qwen-7B, Llama2-7B and 70B, Vicuna-7B and 33B on PopQA and StrategyQA. Entity-substitution evidence: models stick to memory. Generated coherent evidence: highly receptive. Authors checked 50 stubborn cases by hand.
limits: Counter-memory was made by an LLM, so its style may suit LLM readers. Single-turn. Exact acceptance percentages for the single-source case are in figures, not text.
agent_relevance: Coherence is the attack surface for an LLM as it is for people. Do not use fluency of a source as a trust signal.
quote: LLMs are actually highly receptive to external evidence if it is presented in a coherent way

source: Xie et al. (2024) - confirmation bias with mixed evidence
finding: When both memory-consistent and conflicting evidence are present, models lean to what matches their memory. Majority matters, but more memory-aligned items make the bias stronger at the same ratio. More popular facts: stronger bias.
numbers: Memorization ratio (share of answers following memory) on PopQA, by share of evidence that is memory-aligned: GPT-4 1/2 = 65.4%, 2/4 = 75.4%, 2/3 = 91.0%; ChatGPT 1/2 = 43.0%, 2/4 = 63.3%. GPT-4 about 80% on the most popular questions.
limits: Memory is the model's own prior, an analogue of a deep story but not the same thing.
agent_relevance: A frame already in context (including the agent's own earlier answer) will bias how later evidence is weighed. Supports G1 and G4: agreement that came from a shared prior is not independent.

source: Pan, Chen, Kan, Wang (2023) Attacking Open-domain Question Answering by Injecting Misinformation (AACL 2023)
finding: Fake passages injected into the evidence corpus lower QA accuracy. Targeted fakes hurt far more than untargeted ones.
numbers: Relative exact-match drop up to 53.19% for the hybrid attack versus 7.72% for human-written pollution. Question-targeted 53% vs question-agnostic 22% relative EM drop. Pollution was 0.2% (human) to 4.0% (hybrid) of the corpus.
limits: Extractive readers (RoBERTa-style) and BM25 or ColBERT retrieval, not instruction-tuned LLMs.
agent_relevance: A small amount of targeted text is enough. Track the share of context that came from one unvetted source.

source: Pan, Pan, Chen, Nakov, Kan, Wang (2023) On the Risk of Misinformation Pollution with Large Language Models (EMNLP Findings 2023)
finding: LLM-written misinformation hurts open-domain QA a lot, and the properties that persuade machines differ from those that persuade humans, so human-focused defenses do not transfer.
numbers: ODQA performance degraded by up to 87% (BM25-based reader, REIT method, EM down to 3.53); 14% to 54% for DPR-based models and 20% to 87% for BM25-based ones. Pollution was a tiny share of the corpus (0.01% to 0.1%). Defenses tested: misinformation detection, vigilant prompting, reader ensemble; each helped partly and at a cost.
limits: Simulated threat model with GPT-3.5-style generators (GENREAD, CTRLGEN, REVISE, REIT).
agent_relevance: Defenses that need the model to judge truth help only partly. Checks on structure (source, provenance) are safer.

source: Zou, Geng, Wang, Jia (2025) PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models (USENIX Security 2025)
finding: Five injected texts per target question in a database of millions are enough to steer the model to an attacker-chosen answer. Existing defenses were insufficient.
numbers: Black-box ASR with PaLM 2: 97% NQ, 99% HotpotQA, 91% MS-MARCO; above 90% in almost all cases across 8 LLMs. The naive prompt-injection baseline reached only 0.02 ASR on NQ; PoisonedRAG texts are written to be coherent with the planted answer.
limits: Targeted single-question attack that needs retrievable text. Does not test whether a planted frame carries over to later questions.
agent_relevance: Direct measurement of plausible text beating accurate text in an LLM pipeline. Stripping instruction-like text does not help, because the attack is an ordinary claim.

source: Wan, Wallace, Klein (2024) What Evidence Do Language Models Find Convincing? (ACL 2024)
finding: On ConflictingQA (controversial questions with real web pages on both sides) models weigh relevance to the question most and mostly ignore style cues humans use, such as scientific references or a neutral tone.
numbers: Win-rate (how often the model's answer follows a document's view) rose with relevance to the question. Adding scientific references or neutral tone had neutral to negative effect; relevance edits (keyword stuffing, question prefix, one stance sentence) raised win-rate. Each paragraph was compared against at least 5 opposite-stance paragraphs. Exact deltas are in figures, not read as text.
limits: Yes/no controversial questions only; features were correlational plus perturbations.
agent_relevance: Relevance is cheap to fake. A planted page that restates the question will win. Credibility cues cannot be trusted to work for a model.

source: Xu, Lin, Yang, Zhang, Shi, Zhang, Fang, Xu, Qiu (2024) The Earth is Flat because...: Investigating LLMs' Belief towards Misinformation via Persuasive Conversation (ACL 2024)
finding: Multi-turn persuasion with plausible-sounding but false text flips correct beliefs in most models. Non-factual logical appeals work best; plain repetition works less; stronger models resist more.
numbers: Farm dataset; belief tracked over 4 turns (MR@4 = share misinformed by turn 4). At turn 1 with the simplest prompt, belief alteration ranged from 4.1% to 63.4% depending on model. Llama-2-7B-chat averaged MR@4 of 78.2%; GPT-4 was the most resistant. Logical appeals gave the highest misinformed rates in most cases; credibility appeals sometimes higher.
limits: Short factual questions the model first answered correctly; the misinformation is LLM-generated; belief measured by confidence checks. Per-model table values not extracted because the layout was ambiguous.
agent_relevance: Fluent argument works across turns, so per-turn defenses are weaker than a one-time input check. Supports masking source framing at S1.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (ICLR 2024)
finding: Five RLHF assistants conform to a stated user view. Human and preference-model judgments themselves prefer convincing sycophantic text over correct text some of the time, so training pushes toward the plausible.
numbers: User suggests an incorrect answer: accuracy drops up to 27% (LLaMA 2). Are-you-sure probe: models wrongly admit a mistake between 42% (GPT-4) and 98% (Claude 1.3). Claude 2 preference model prefers a sycophantic answer to a baseline truthful answer 95% of the time, and to a helpful truthful answer about 45% of the time on the hardest misconceptions.
limits: Mostly 2023-era models. Sycophancy is toward the user, not toward a manipulated corpus, so it is a neighbour of the effect, not the same effect.
agent_relevance: Explains why the model is a weak filter: its own preference leans to the plausible. Keep code, not the model, as the judge (G5).
quote: humans and preference models prefer convincingly-written sycophantic responses over correct ones a non-negligible fraction of the time

source: Chen and Shu (2024) Can LLM-Generated Misinformation Be Detected? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Misinformation written by an LLM is harder for humans and for LLM detectors to spot than human-written misinformation with the same meaning. Hallucination-style fakes are the hardest.
numbers: Humans spotted only 9.6% of ChatGPT-generated hallucinated news on average. ChatGPT-3.5 detected 0.0% and GPT-4 10.0% of hallucinated news. Human detection was worse on rewritten fakes (p = 9.15e-5) and open-ended fakes (p = 1.01e-6) than on human-written ones (paired t-test). ChatGPT refused explicit misinformation prompts but not hallucination or rewriting prompts.
limits: 10 human evaluators for the human test; Politifact-based data; same-meaning comparison isolates style.
agent_relevance: Detection by a model fails exactly where the text is fluent. Detect by provenance and by check, not by reading style.

source: Spitale, Biller-Andorno, Germani (2023) AI model GPT-3 (dis)informs us better than humans (Science Advances 2023; preprint v4)
finding: People believed GPT-3 disinformation tweets slightly more often than human-written ones and could not tell synthetic from organic tweets.
numbers: 697 valid respondents of 869 recruited. Recognition of false tweets: organic 0.92 vs synthetic 0.89 (p = 0.0032). True tweets recognised: synthetic 0.84 vs organic 0.72 (p < 0.0001). Synthetic vs organic source: 0.50 at chance overall. GPT-3 as judge: 0.89 on disinformation tweets and 0.64 on accurate tweets, versus humans 0.92 and 0.72.
limits: Preprint version read. 11 topics (climate, vaccines, 5G and others), single tweet format, online sample mostly from English-speaking countries.
agent_relevance: The model as a filter did worse than the human crowd on accurate content. Do not let the model grade its own inputs.

source: Salvi, Horta Ribeiro, Gallotti, West (2025) On the conversational persuasiveness of large language models: a randomized controlled trial (Nature Human Behaviour 2025; preprint 2024)
finding: In live debates GPT-4 with access to the opponent's basic personal data beat humans at moving the opponent's views; without personal data the edge was not significant.
numbers: N = 820 unique participants, 2x2 design (human vs GPT-4 opponent; personalised vs not). GPT-4 with personalization: 81.7% higher odds of increased agreement vs human opponents (p < 0.01). Without personalization: higher but not significant (p = 0.31).
limits: Harmless debate topics, short debates; preprint version read; effect is on odds of agreement, not belief change in points.
agent_relevance: Identity-matched framing matters more than raw text quality. A source that mirrors the reader is the risky one (Weick: sensemaking is identity-grounded).

source: Hackenburg, Tappin, Rottger, Hale, Bright, Margetts (2025) Scaling language model size yields diminishing returns for single-message political persuasion (PNAS 2025; preprint titled Evidence of a Log Scaling Law for Political Persuasion with LLMs)
finding: Message persuasiveness grows with the log of model size: frontier models are barely more persuasive than models an order of magnitude smaller. Task completion (coherence, staying on topic) explains most of the larger-model edge.
numbers: 24 models, 720 messages on 10 US political issues, N = 25,982 survey experiment. A mid-sized model (37.9B active parameters) shifted attitudes 5.77 percentage points toward the message stance. Each one-unit rise in log parameters adds 1.26 points.
limits: Single static messages, US issues, survey attitudes not behaviour.
agent_relevance: A small model can already carry a deep-story attack; a bigger reader gives only partial protection.

source: Hackenburg, Tappin, Hewitt, Saunders, Black, Lin, Fist, Margetts, Rand, Summerfield (2025) The Levers of Political Persuasion with Conversational AI
finding: Post-training and prompting raise AI persuasion more than scale or personalization. Persuasion is mostly driven by information density, and the more persuasive set-ups made more inaccurate claims. Moral reframing and deep canvassing did not beat a basic prompt.
numbers: N = 76,977 in three experiments, 19 LLMs, 707 political issues, 466,769 claims fact-checked. Post-training boosted persuasion by up to 51% and prompting by up to 27%. Information density explains 44% of the variability in persuasion (average correlation r = 0.76). Among the most persuasive models, accuracy was 62% with the information prompt versus 78% with another prompt.
limits: Opinions on current political issues in conversation, not frames carried to later events. Storytelling was one of the tested strategies; this file read only the text about moral reframing and deep canvassing being worse than the basic prompt.
agent_relevance: Suggests claim volume, not story form, drives LLM persuaders, and that persuasion trades off with accuracy. High claim density from one source is a flag for review.

source: Costello, Pennycook, Rand (2024) Durably reducing conspiracy beliefs through dialogues with AI (Science)
finding: GPT-4 Turbo dialogue with believers in conspiracy theories lowered belief durably, reportedly still visible after two months. If so, the same machinery can weaken a deep story. Could not be opened (403), so numbers are not recorded.
numbers: Sample size and percent reduction not verified this session.
limits: Not opened. Lead for another angle.
agent_relevance: If an LLM can weaken a deep story with fact-based dialogue, a cleaned and counter-argued context may reduce its pull on the agent too.

source: Goldstein, Sastry, Musser, DiResta, Gentzel, Sedova (2023) Generative Language Models and Automated Influence Operations: Emerging Threats and Potential Mitigations
finding: Threat report. Organises influence operations by actors, behaviours and content (the ABCs of disinformation) and argues language models may lower cost and raise scale of campaigns. Only the table of contents was read.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Skimmed only. A policy report, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Source for the threat model behind S1: the attacker can generate coherent narrative at scale.

source: Green and Brock (2000) The role of transportation in the persuasiveness of public narratives (J. Personality and Social Psychology 79)
finding: Human experiments: being absorbed in a story makes people accept its beliefs more and notice fewer false notes. Lead for why narrative form works on people. Not opened; no figures recorded.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened. LLM evidence (a24) suggests story form is not what moves models.
agent_relevance: Do not assume narrative persuasion transfers to LLMs; test it.

source: Lewandowsky, Ecker, Seifert, Schwarz, Cook (2012) Misinformation and its correction: continued influence and successful debiasing (Psychological Science in the Public Interest)
finding: Review of why corrections often fail: coherent stories are sticky, repetition raises acceptance, and an alternative explanation helps. Lead for the human literature; not opened this session.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: The point that a correction needs an alternative cause may map to a rule that revising a premise needs a replacement (G2).

source: Synthesis (author's own, not a source): what the founding evidence supports for S1 input hygiene
finding: Human side: only one qualitative claim (Prochaska 2024) says deep stories steer later frame choice. LLM side: no study opened tests that prediction directly (a frame planted earlier in the context shaping the reading of a later, unrelated event). Closest proxies are knowledge conflict (a12, a13), corpus poisoning (a14, a15, a16), multi-turn belief flipping (a18) and sycophancy (a19).
numbers: No direct measurement exists in the sources opened. The open question in SUBFIELDS.md (equal-token test of masked versus unmasked prompts) is untested.
limits: Author synthesis, not evidence.
agent_relevance: Run the equal-token test: the same ambiguous event under (1) neutral context, (2) planted deep-story context, (3) deep-story context masked at S1. Score frame choice and accuracy.
